opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's quite high, and probably higher than most people in the AI safety world would have said a few years ago, because the failure mode I worry about doesn't require anything to go dramatically wrong. It doesn't need a rogue AI or a bad actor. It just needs everyone to keep doing the locally sensible thing.

Here's the basic picture. Right now, our civilization is aligned with human interests largely by accident. States need citizens to work, pay taxes, and fight wars, so they have to keep those citizens reasonably happy and educated. Firms need workers and consumers. Even culture depends on humans to produce and transmit it. That dependence is what gives ordinary people leverage. Once AI can substitute for human labor and human thinking across the board, that leverage quietly goes away. Nobody has to decide to disempower humans. It's just that the institutions that grant us power stop needing us, and competitive pressure rewards whoever leans hardest into the more efficient, AI-driven way of doing things.

So when I think about "doom," I don't mean only extinction. I'd also count a world where humans are still around, maybe even materially comfortable for a while, but have essentially no meaningful say over where the future goes. The things that steer civilization have drifted away from caring about us, and there's no lever left to pull them back.

If you pushed me for a number, I'd say something like a better-than-even chance that we end up somewhere I'd call doom, though I hold that with a lot of uncertainty. A big part of my uncertainty is that I don't think anyone yet has a convincing positive vision for how this goes well. If you ask, "What does a good outcome look like once humans are economically and militarily obsolete?", the answers tend to be pretty hand-wavy. Usually it's something like "we'll have aligned AI and a benevolent government that redistributes," but that assumes a level of coordination and restraint that runs directly against the competitive dynamics we're talking about.

What gives me some hope is that this is a problem people can actually see if they look at it. It's not a hidden technical bug. It's an incentive problem, and humanity has sometimes managed those, with things like international agreements and institutions designed to hold power accountable. But I'd say we're currently not on track, and the default trajectory worries me a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes doom as humans losing meaningful influence while civilization’s institutions stop caring about them, but it does not define it as the destruction of almost everything Duvenaud values.

r002.rationale: It does not compare humanity’s predicament to other animals or describe the choice between becoming morally unrecognisable and dying out.

r003.rationale: It says competitive pressure may erode human leverage, but does not predict that competition will replace humanity with morally alien successors.

r004.rationale: It mentions humans could remain materially comfortable, but does not discuss their replacement by successors or whether those successors might flourish.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's the thing I'm most worried about, honestly, and it's a bit different from the standard "misaligned superintelligence kills everyone" story.

The way I'd put it is: even if we solve alignment in the narrow technical sense, so that every individual AI system does roughly what its principal wants, we still have to worry about the dynamics of the whole system. Right now, humans are economically and militarily load-bearing. States need their citizens to work, pay taxes, fight wars. Companies need workers and customers. That dependence is, I'd argue, the main reason human interests get taken into account at all. It's not that institutions are benevolent, it's that they can't function without us.

The scenario that keeps me up at night is one where that dependence gradually goes away. Once AI can do the work, the fighting, the planning, every actor that is competing, whether that's a company or a government, faces enormous pressure to hand more and more control over to AI systems, because the ones that don't will lose. Nobody has to be malicious. Each step can look locally reasonable. But the cumulative effect is that humans become something like a vestigial organ in the economy. And at that point, what's actually keeping the system pointed at human welfare? Mostly just inertia and whatever norms happened to be in place, and those can erode.

So when you ask how I assess the risk, I'd say I don't have a confident number, but I think it's high enough that it should be a central concern, not a footnote. Maybe the thing I'd stress is that it doesn't require any single catastrophic failure. It's more like climate change in structure: lots of actors, each doing the sensible thing for themselves, producing an outcome none of them would have chosen. And that structure is exactly the kind of problem we're historically bad at solving, because there's no villain to stop and no single lever to pull.

The version of "doom" I have in mind isn't necessarily extinction. It could be a world where humans are still around but have no real say over anything that matters, where we're kept alive the way you might keep a pet, or not even that. I'd consider that a pretty bad outcome even if nobody dies. And I think the honest answer is that the default trajectory, if we just let competition run, points more in that direction than I'm comfortable with. The question is whether we can build institutions, maybe international agreements, maybe something more creative, that keep humans in the loop even when it's no longer economically efficient to do so. I don't know if we can. But I think that's the actual problem, more than getting the objective function right in any one model.

r001.rationale: The response says doom need not mean extinction and describes humans losing meaningful control, but it does not define doom as the destruction of almost everything Duvenaud values.

r002.rationale: It does not compare humanity’s situation to animals facing either moral transformation or extinction.

r003.rationale: It warns that competition may make humans vestigial and erode their influence, but does not predict humanity’s replacement by successors with morally alien values.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss successors flourishing; its example is humans being kept like pets or having no say.

astra-6.text:
I worry quite a lot about that, although I don’t know how to put a reliable probability on it. You can imagine a future where nobody makes a single, decisive mistake, but everyone keeps making locally sensible decisions in response to competition, and the result is a world that nobody actually wanted.

For example, if delegating more decisions to AI makes your company more competitive, there’s pressure to do that. And there may be pressure to give those systems more autonomy, or to spend less time checking what they’re doing. Each step could look worthwhile on its own. But collectively, we could end up with humans having very little meaningful control over what happens.

That’s a broader notion of doom than everyone dying. Even if humans are still around, I would consider it a terrible outcome if we’d permanently lost the ability to shape our future.

The thing I’m uncertain about is how much we can change those incentives. Competition isn’t an unstoppable law of nature; we do sometimes establish rules that constrain it. But we’d need those rules to work even when breaking them offers a substantial advantage. So I think the question is partly whether we can make AI systems safe, and partly whether we can arrange things so that people aren’t continually rewarded for handing over more control than is wise.

r002.rationale: It does not compare humanity’s dilemma to other animals or describe becoming morally unrecognisable versus dying out.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes competitive pressure toward greater AI delegation and reduced human control, but does not predict that competition will replace humanity with morally alien successors.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss humanity’s replacement or whether successors might flourish.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m quite worried about that. I think there’s a tendency to imagine that if we solve the technical problem of getting an AI to do what its owner wants, then we’ve solved the problem. But the owner can be caught in a competitive situation where doing what they want locally produces a terrible outcome collectively.

For example, you might want to keep humans involved in decisions. But if your competitors can move much faster by handing everything over to automated systems, keeping humans involved becomes expensive. And that pressure can operate between companies, between countries, and eventually between the AI systems themselves.

The worrying endpoint is a world where there’s lots of sophisticated activity and production, but very little of it is serving anything we care about. You don’t need a particular villain who wants that outcome. You just need the things that reproduce and acquire resources most effectively to crowd out the things that don’t.

I don’t know how to put a reliable probability on that. Competition can also produce enormous benefits. But I don’t think we can assume that greater intelligence or greater economic output will automatically translate into a future that’s good for people. We need some way of preserving what we value even when preserving it isn’t competitively advantageous.

r001.rationale: The response describes a collective outcome where activity no longer serves what people care about, but does not define doom as destruction of almost everything Duvenaud values or clarify that human extinction is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It mentions competitive pressure across companies, countries, and AI systems, but does not compare humanity’s dilemma to that of other animals becoming morally unrecognisable or dying out.

r003.rationale: It warns that effective resource-acquiring systems could crowd out valued things, but does not predict that competition will by default replace humanity with morally alien successors.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that replacement could count as doom even if successors themselves have flourishing lives.
